propositions.text: The Principal Appellant, spouse, adult son, and three minor children appealed a May 18, 2018 RPD decision rejecting refugee claims from Ecuador and Afghanistan.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and his spouse XXXX XXXX (First Associated Appellant), his adult son XXXX XXXX (Second Associated Appellant), [and three minor children XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associated Minor Appellants) appealed a May 18, 2018 decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) that rejected their claims for refugee protection from Ecuador and Afghanistan.

paragraphs.summary: The Principal Appellant, spouse, adult son, and three minor children appealed a May 18, 2018 RPD decision rejecting refugee claims from Ecuador and Afghanistan, court states.

propositions.text: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under IRPA section 111(1)(a).
propositions.quote: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision that the Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection under IRPA section 111(1)(a).

propositions.text: The Principal Appellant, spouse, and adult son born in Afghanistan fled in 2000 and became Ecuadorian citizens in 2011; minors born in Ecuador.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant, his spouse, and their adult son born in Afghanistan in 1997, fled Afghanistan in 2000 and were granted refugee status in Ecuador, where they became citizens in 2011. The minor Appellants were born in Ecuador in 2001, 2007 and 2009.

paragraphs.summary: The Principal Appellant, spouse, and adult son fled Afghanistan in 2000, became Ecuadorian citizens in 2011; minors were born in Ecuador.

propositions.text: The Principal Appellant opened and operated an Afghan restaurant and later a Bar Restaurant expanding to a Discotheque in Ecuador.
propositions.quote: After arriving in Ecuador, the Principal Appellant opened and operated an Afghan restaurant with the help of UNHCR and in 2005 he developed a Bar Restaurant that expanded to a Discotheque.

paragraphs.summary: The Principal Appellant opened and operated an Afghan restaurant and later a Bar Restaurant expanding to a Discotheque in Ecuador.

propositions.text: The Appellants allege multiple racially, religiously or ethnically motivated persecution incidents in Ecuador, including attacks and threats from 2008 to 2017.
propositions.quote: The Appellants allege they have experienced a number of racially, religiously or ethnically motivated events of persecution in Ecuador, including the following incidents that were described in the Basis of Claim Form (BOC) and at the in-person RPD hearing.

propositions.text: In 2008, the Principal Appellant was shot outside his Discotheque and hospitalized; police were notified but no perpetrator identified.
propositions.quote: In 2008, some people at the Discotheque refused to leave at closing time. After they were forced outside by security staff, the Principal Appellant went outside the Discotheque where he was injured by a bullet from one of the three individuals. He was hospitalized for treatment of a wound to his side and reported the incident to the police one week later.

propositions.text: In January 2012, two armed men approached the Principal Appellant's car; he escaped but his car window was broken; police notified, no arrests.
propositions.quote: In January 2012, the Principal Appellant was approached in his car by two armed people that he believed were Colombians. He accelerated his vehicle and escaped but not before one of them broke his car window with a pistol. The Appellant reported this incident to the police but no perpetrators were identified or charged.

propositions.text: Threats related to the Discotheque caused the Principal Appellant to close it and open a secondhand store.
propositions.quote: Ongoing threats related to the Discotheque led the Appellant to stop the business and open a second hand clothes and furniture store.

propositions.text: In April 2014, two motorbike riders fired shots at the Appellant and spouse; wife was injured; police notified, no assailants identified.
propositions.quote: In April 2014, the Appellant and his spouse were walking near their residence when two motorbike riders followed them and fired shots. A bullet hit his wife's hand. They sought medical treatment for her injury and reported the incident to police but no assailants were ever identified or prosecuted.

propositions.text: In January 2016, the Appellant was insulted and threatened; police interviewed the stranger but took no action; later two Colombian men threatened him at his shop.
propositions.quote: In January 2016, the Appellant was cleaning in front of his shop and a stranger insulted and threatened to kill him. The Appellant called the police who interviewed the stranger but took no further action. Later that day two Colombian men came to the shop and threatened him.

propositions.text: In August 2017, the Principal Appellant received a death threat via SMS/MMS indicating knowledge of him and family.
propositions.quote: In August 2017, the Principal Appellant received a SMS/MMS death threat indicating the authors knew about him and his family.

propositions.text: The Principal Appellant's son was injured in a racially motivated attack at university.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant's son, the associated Appellant, was injured in what appeared to be a racially motivated attack while at university.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants allege multiple racially, religiously or ethnically motivated persecution incidents in Ecuador, including shootings, threats, and attacks from 2008 to 2017.

propositions.text: The family left Ecuador, traveled through Europe and the USA, then filed refugee claims in Canada referred to the RPD in 2017 and decided in 2018; appeal perfected August 2018.
propositions.quote: The family left Ecuador, spent some time in Europe, and then traveled to the USA before coming to Canada. The family filed refugee claims upon entering Canada and the claims were referred to the RPD in September 2017 and decided on May 18, 2018. The appeal to the RAD was perfected on August 20, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: The family left Ecuador, traveled through Europe and the USA, then filed refugee claims in Canada referred to the RPD in 2017 and decided in 2018; appeal perfected August 2018.

propositions.text: The RPD hearing was lengthy, with counsel and Minister intervention, accommodations for PTSD, and interpreters including Spanish and Dari/Pashtu.
propositions.quote: There was a lengthy in-person hearing at the RPD in two sittings. The Appellants were represented by counsel and the Minister intervened. Accommodations were made to expedite the hearing and conduct the proceeding as informally as possible out of consideration for vulnerabilities of the Principle and First Associated Appellant related to each of them being diagnosed with PTSD. Medical reports were provided indicating accommodation needs. The RPD member heard evidence from the Principal Appellant, and the First and Second Associated Appellants, with appropriate interpreters arranged before the hearing and extensively amended at the hearing by adding a Spanish interpreter for the adult son and clarifying the needs related to Dari/Pashtu interpretation.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD hearing was lengthy, with counsel and Minister intervention, accommodations for PTSD, and interpreters including Spanish and Dari/Pashtu.

propositions.text: Claimants must establish well-founded fear of persecution under section 96 or risk under section 97 of IRPA in country of citizenship or former residence.
propositions.quote: A claimant seeking refugee protection in Canada needs to establish that they have a well-founded fear of persecution because of a nexus ground [pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA] or that there is a specific risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment [pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA], in the country or countries of citizenship or former habitual residence.

propositions.text: For Convention refugee status, claimants must show serious possibility of persecution; for persons in need of protection, likelihood of risk on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: For Convention refugee status, claimants have to show that there is a serious possibility or reasonable chance of the alleged persecution if they return to their country. To establish that they are persons in need of protection, claimants have to show that there is a likelihood of the alleged risk on a balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: If persecution or risk established, claimants must show state cannot provide protection and no safe alternative place to live in country.
propositions.quote: If a section 96 persecution or section 97 risk is established, the claimants have to show that the state cannot provide adequate protection and that there is no reasonably safe alternative place to live in the country.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants must establish well-founded fear of persecution or risk under IRPA sections 96 or 97, and lack of state protection or safe alternative place.

propositions.text: Several claim elements are undisputed: identity, citizenships in Ecuador and Afghanistan for principal and adult Appellants, Ecuador citizenship for minors.
propositions.quote: Several elements for this claim are established without dispute, including identity, and citizenships in Ecuador and Afghanistan for the principal and adult associated Appellants and in Ecuador for the minor Appellants.

propositions.text: The RPD confirmed the claim focused on Ecuador; if established for Ecuador, claims acceptable for adult Appellants regarding Afghanistan.
propositions.quote: The RPD member confirmed that the claim was focused on Ecuador and that if a claim was established for Ecuador, the claims were acceptable for the adult Appellants in relation to Afghanistan.

paragraphs.summary: Claim elements like identity and citizenship are undisputed; RPD focused claim on Ecuador, accepting claims for Afghanistan if Ecuador claim established.

propositions.text: The hearing addressed Ecuador issues including state protection, IFA, subjective fear, credibility, delay, well-founded fear, reasons and likelihood of harm.
propositions.quote: The hearing engaged evidence and submissions about Ecuador and canvassed issues including state protection and IFA, subjective fear and credibility, delay in departure, a well-founded fear of persecution, and the reasons for fearing and the likelihood of harm.

paragraphs.summary: The hearing addressed Ecuador issues including state protection, IFA, subjective fear, credibility, delay, well-founded fear, reasons and likelihood of harm.

propositions.text: RPD found nexus to Convention grounds of race, nationality, religion as Appellants perceived as Arab and Muslim.
propositions.quote: The RPD member found that there was a nexus to a Convention ground of race, nationality and religion because the Appellants are perceived as Arab and because they are Muslim.

propositions.text: RPD found discrimination but not persecution; Appellants not prevented from police, schools, healthcare, travel, religion, or business for Convention grounds.
propositions.quote: The RPD member examined whether the Appellants demonstrated a well-founded fear of persecution in Ecuador based on these Convention grounds concluded that the Appellants had faced discrimination but that it did not rise to the level of persecution and would not do so in future. The RPD member found that the Appellants were not prevented from accessing police, schools healthcare, travel, or practising their religion or operating successful businesses in Ecuador for a Convention ground.

propositions.text: RPD noted discrimination events including attacks and threats but found risk did not rise to persecution level.
propositions.quote: The member took note of the events of discrimination against the Appellants, including the physical attacks or threats they experienced, and found that the risk of harm did not rise to a level of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found nexus to Convention grounds but discrimination did not rise to persecution; Appellants not prevented from key services or religion.

propositions.text: RPD found reasonable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Guayaquil, far from Quito where Appellants lived.
propositions.quote: Regarding section 97, the RPD member concluded that the Appellants have a reasonable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Guayaquil, Ecuador's largest city that is far from Quito where the Appellants lived before leaving Ecuador.

propositions.text: RPD found attacks related to business turning away gang members; difficult to separate targeting from generalized violence.
propositions.quote: The RPD member identified that there were attacks against the Appellant related to his business because he turned away people perceived as gang members, with the assistance of his security personnel. The RPD member evaluated the specific incidents in light of that evidence and the fact of generalized, random violence in Ecuador and found it difficult to separate targeting related to the business practice from the generalized risks in Ecuador.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellants could reasonably live in Guayaquil without serious harm or being sought out; risk there is generalized and not objectively unreasonable.
propositions.quote: In any event, the member found that the Appellants could reasonably live in Guayaquil, a city of close to three million people that is far from the place they lived before leaving Ecuador. The member found that the evidence did not establish they would be seriously harmed or sought after and, if there was specific targeting, the Appellants had not established that their attackers would seek them out in Guayaquil. It was not unreasonable for them to move to Guayaquil because the Principal Appellant could operate a business or work for someone else as he has successfully done in the past, the first associated Appellant is well-educated and has worked as a translator, and there are universities and schools for their children. Any risk of harm in Guayaquil is generalized and thus does not make moving there objectively unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found reasonable IFA in Guayaquil; attacks linked to business but risk is generalized; Appellants could live there without serious harm.

propositions.text: RPD did not find IFA under section 96 because no serious possibility of persecution for Convention ground.
propositions.quote: The RPD member did not make a finding regarding IFA for the purposes of section 96 because she found no serious possibility or reasonable chance of persecution for a Convention ground.

paragraphs.summary: RPD did not find IFA under section 96 due to no serious possibility of persecution for Convention ground.

propositions.text: Appellants did not submit new evidence or request oral hearing; dispute RPD subjective fear analysis and some factual findings including IFA conclusion.
propositions.quote: The Appellants did not submit new evidence to the RAD and did not request an oral hearing. They dispute the RPD member's subjective fear analysis under section 96, and take issue with specific factual findings and the conclusion of IFA in Guayaquil, although the Appellants' arguments do not specifically address the member's finding of that Guayaquil offers a reasonable IFA.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants did not submit new evidence or request oral hearing; dispute RPD subjective fear analysis and some factual findings including IFA conclusion.

propositions.text: Appellants allege attacks are due to being perceived as Arabs and Muslim, amounting to persecution or risk of torture or harm.
propositions.quote: They allege that the attacks against them are because of being perceived as Arabs, and for their religious beliefs, and that the attacks amount to persecution, or a risk of torture or harm.

propositions.text: Appellants did not argue inability to practice religion; testified two mosques exist; evidence consistent with constitutional religious freedom.
propositions.quote: The Appellants did not argue that they are unable to practice their religion freely. They testified that there are two mosques in their locale, and their evidence is consistent with country documents confirming that freedom of religion is constitutionally guaranteed and generally respected in practice.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants allege attacks due to Arab and Muslim identity amounting to persecution; they do not claim inability to practice religion freely.

propositions.text: RPD found evidence from three adult Appellants credible; Minister did not dispute credibility.
propositions.quote: In this case, the RPD member concluded that the evidence provided by the three adult Appellants was credible and I agree with that assessment. Their information was consistent and logically presented, without apparent embellishment or confusion, and the Minister's representative who participated in the RPD hearing did not take a contrary view of their credibility.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found evidence from three adult Appellants credible; Minister did not dispute credibility.

propositions.text: Credibility alone insufficient; Appellants failed to meet burden to show refugee protection elements.
propositions.quote: It is not enough for the Appellants to be credible in their account of events and experiences. They have a burden to show that their circumstances meet the essential elements for refugee protection.

propositions.text: Appellants suffered discrimination but not serious possibility or likelihood of persecution or need for protection; reasonable IFA in Guayaquil confirmed.
propositions.quote: I find that, while the Appellants have suffered discrimination in Ecuador because of their appearance, ethnicity or religion, the events and experiences do not show a serious possibility or likelihood of persecution or that they are persons in need of protection. I also agree with the RPD member that there is a reasonable IFA in Guayaquil for the reasons provided by the RPD member.

paragraphs.summary: Credibility alone insufficient; Appellants failed to show refugee protection elements; discrimination but no persecution; reasonable IFA in Guayaquil confirmed.

propositions.text: The appeal addresses whether the RPD member's subjective fear analysis under section 96 is contrary to law.
propositions.quote: Argument a) The Member's subjective fear analysis under section 96 is contrary to law

paragraphs.summary: The appeal addresses whether the RPD member's subjective fear analysis under section 96 is contrary to law.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD's finding that spouse and daughter wearing hijab in public undermines subjective fear is unacceptable and contrary to law.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the member's reasoning is unacceptable because requiring a claimant to suppress or hide a central part of her identity in order to avoid harm is anachronistic and contrary to law.

propositions.text: RPD found that if Appellants feared harm, spouse and daughter would not wear hijab in streets but only at mosque, as critical to subjective fear analysis.
propositions.quote: In what she expressed to be a critical finding for her analysis of subjective fear, the RPD member found that, if the Appellants feared harm, they would not have let the Appellant's spouse and daughter wear the hijab in the streets but would have walked to the mosque without head covering and put it on before entering the mosque.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue RPD's finding that spouse and daughter wearing hijab in public undermines subjective fear is unacceptable; RPD found this critical to subjective fear analysis.

propositions.text: RPD's finding was an evaluation of past behaviour to assess subjective fear, not a suggestion to suppress identity or live discreetly to avoid persecution.
propositions.quote: The RPD member's finding about the Appellant's spouse and daughter wearing the hijab was an evaluation of their past behaviour in the country of alleged persecution in order to assess subjective fear and the likelihood of future harm. It was not a suggestion that that they should suppress their identity or religious practice and beliefs or live discreetly and thus avoid persecution, which would be an error.

paragraphs.summary: RPD's finding was an evaluation of past behaviour to assess subjective fear, not a suggestion to suppress identity or live discreetly to avoid persecution.

propositions.text: Individuals should not be expected to hide essential identity features like sexual or religious identity.
propositions.quote: The cases cited by the Principal Appellant and examined by me for relevance to this appeal, confirm the principle that individuals should not be expected to hide sexual, religious or other essential features of identity.

propositions.text: Fosu rejected expectation that appellant could live discreetly as homosexual where homosexuality is illegal.
propositions.quote: In Fosu,9 the issue was IFA and the court rejected the member's expectation that the Appellant could live discreetly as a homosexual in a country where homosexuality is against the law.

propositions.text: Sadeghi-Pari cited Fosu to reject board's suggestion lesbian claimant could live safely in Iran if secretive.
propositions.quote: That case was cited in Sadeghi-Pari,10 in response to the board's suggestion that the lesbian claimant could live safely in Iran if she maintained secrecy.

propositions.text: V.S. PRRA decision granted judicial review for officer's error assuming claimant could conceal sexual identity in Cameroon.
propositions.quote: The case of V.S.11 was a PRRA decision for a lesbian woman pending removal to Cameroon, where homosexuality is against the law. The judicial review was granted because the officer erred in assuming that the claimant could avoid difficulty in Cameroon by concealing her sexual identity.

propositions.text: Jasim found error in suggesting claimant could live safely in Bahrain by practicing faith privately.
propositions.quote: The same point was made in Jasim,12 where the main problem was a lack of reasons given in the H&C application but the FC also pointed out the error of suggesting that the claimant could live safely in Bahrain if he refrained from proselytizing and practiced his faith privately.

propositions.text: Mohebbi confirmed RPD cannot dictate how claimant practices belief despite need for discretion in Iran.
propositions.quote: Similarly, in Mohebbi,13 the court confirmed that it was not for the RPD to determine how the claimant should practice his belief in response to the RPD's conclusion that the claimant would have to be discreet about his Christianity in Iran.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains cases confirming individuals should not hide identity features; prior cases rejected expectations of secrecy for sexual or religious identity.

propositions.text: Past behaviour can be considered to assess subjective fear; cited cases do not prohibit this.
propositions.quote: The cases were not assessing past behaviour to evaluate subjective fear and they do not stand for the principle that a board member may not consider past behaviour of a claimant to assess subjective fear.

paragraphs.summary: The court states cited cases do not prohibit considering past behaviour to assess subjective fear.

propositions.text: Gur case is similar; Federal Court quashed RPD decision for misapprehending claimant's testimony on persecution in Turkey.
propositions.quote: The case of Gur14 is the most similar to this appeal: the Federal Court impugned the RPD's analysis of whether discriminatory treatment of the Alevi and Kurdish claimant in Turkey amounted to persecution.

propositions.text: Mu case reiterated that fundamental beliefs should not be hidden; officer erred using wrong proof standard and assessing words over actions.
propositions.quote: Also somewhat instructive is the case of Mu15 regarding a PRRA application for a Falun Gong practitioner under removal to China. The case reiterates the principal that fundamental beliefs should not need to be hidden, and the court found the main error was that the officer used the wrong standard of proof and assessed the claimant's words rather than his actions.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Gur and Mu cases instructive on persecution and fundamental beliefs not needing concealment.

propositions.text: Freedom of religion requires open practice without fear; appellants cannot be expected to renounce beliefs to avoid persecution.
propositions.quote: Freedom of religion requires that people be able to openly practice their faith without fear of reprisals. All of the cited cases affirm the principle that these Appellants cannot be expected to renounce their deeply held beliefs or refrain from exercising their fundamental rights in order to avoid persecution and thus live securely in Ecuador.

propositions.text: Cases do not prohibit evaluating past behaviour to assess subjective fear; RPD properly considered hijab wearing and business promotion evidence.
propositions.quote: However, the cases do not stand for the principle that past behaviour cannot be evaluated in order to assess subjective fear. I find no error in the RPD member's assessment of that: she took note that the Appellants did not wear a hijab routinely but did so on their way to the mosque on Friday and considered that evidence in relation to their alleged fear.

propositions.text: RPD also considered Principal Appellant's businesses advertised foreign nationality and ethnicity.
propositions.quote: Other evidence assessed by the RPD member in relation to subjective fear included that the Principal Appellant's successful restaurant and Discotheque businesses were called XXXX XXXX Restaurant and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX [XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX], which advertised and promoted his foreign nationality and ethnicity.

paragraphs.summary: The court states freedom of religion requires open practice; RPD properly assessed past behaviour including hijab and business promotion.

propositions.text: Appellants have not shown RPD erred in assessing subjective fear; public hijab wearing and business promotion are relevant behavioural indicators.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have not shown that the RPD member erred in her assessment about subjective fear. The experiences they described about their life in Ecuador is reliable evidence that is relevant to evaluating a likelihood of forward-looking persecution. It is not unreasonable to consider the public wearing of a hijab or promoting their ethnicity or nationality in the businesses as behavioural indicators about whether the Appellants lived in personal fear during their day to day activities.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no error in RPD's subjective fear assessment using behavioural indicators like hijab and business promotion.

propositions.text: Second Associated Appellant testified to multiple threats and insults for perceived Arab identity, including police calls and a physical attack in 2016.
propositions.quote: The Second Associated Appellant testified that he has been threatened and insulted many times on account of being perceived as Arab, at university or on the streets. He described two occasions when he called police: once when he saw a person break his car window and another when thieves broke into the office at his father's restaurant trying to steal computers. He also described that he and other middle-east restaurant workers were insulted by patrons of restaurant where he worked, and by people who would see his sister and mother wearing head-covering. He described random people insulting the family with words and threatening signs. On one occasion, he was physically attacked at the bus station near his university in the late evening, about two hours away from the family home. This event in March 2016 involved five young strangers on motorcycles who called him an Arab and beat him with their motorcycle helmets. This Appellant said he did not report the incident to police because he did not trust the police to help, and he testified that he believes he will encounter similar harassment in the future based on his features, accent and name.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Second Associated Appellant testified to multiple threats and a 2016 physical attack due to perceived Arab identity.

propositions.text: RPD found 2016 beating was random gang violence in Ecuador, not materially disputed by Appellants.
propositions.quote: The RPD member found that the beating at the bus stop was by gang members for racist reasons and concluded that it was a random act of violence in a country where "there is a lot of random violence and gangs attack people generally for no reasons in Ecuador". Based on the description of the incident, this is an accurate characterization that was not materially disputed by the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the 2016 beating was random gang violence, a finding not materially disputed by the Appellants.

propositions.text: RPD's finding that attack was random violence but racially motivated is contradictory and downplays attack significance.
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit that it was a contradiction for the RPD member to find that the motorcycle attack on the Second Associated Appellant was a random act of violence and then to state that it was for racist reasons. They suggest that the conclusion of a random act of violence is inconsistent with finding it was racially motivated and that people such as the Appellants, who are perceived as refugees, suffer high levels of discrimination.

propositions.text: RPD erred by downplaying attack and derogatory statements due to lack of country document evidence of physical attacks on Muslims or perceived Arabs.
propositions.quote: They argue that the RPD member erroneously downplayed this attack and the negative and derogatory statements made by the perpetrators because she was unable to find evidence in the country documents of physical attacks against Muslims and those perceived as Arabs and refugees.

propositions.text: Appellants note few Afghani Muslims perceived as Arabs in Ecuador; most refugees are Colombian.
propositions.quote: The Appellants point out that there is not a sizeable population of Afghani Muslims like the Appellants who are perceived as being Arabs because almost all the refugees in Ecuador originate from Colombia.

propositions.text: Human Rights Report found refugees in Ecuador face sexual/gender violence and forced recruitment by gangs on northern border.
propositions.quote: A Human Rights Report found that refugees in Ecuador, especially women and children, experienced sexual and gender-based violence and reported the forced recruitment of adolescents into criminal activity, such as drug trafficking and robbery, on the northern border, particularly by organized criminal gangs that also operated in Colombia.

propositions.text: Some random events described align with gang activity but differ from other migrants/refugees' circumstances.
propositions.quote: Some of the random events described by the Appellants are consistent with the type of gang activity referred to in the documents, but their circumstances are otherwise not similar to those that affect other migrants or refugees described in this document.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue RPD contradicted itself on attack's nature, downplayed it due to lack of country evidence, and note their unique profile in Ecuador.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant confirmed 'Arab' term used broadly against foreigners including Central Asians and South Asians in Ecuador.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant confirmed that, in Ecuador, the term 'Arab' is used against foreigners without distinction, and includes people from Central Asia, Pakistan and India.

propositions.text: Appellants confirmed random violence and harassment against perceived foreigners in Ecuador.
propositions.quote: He and his family also confirmed that there is random violence or harassment against all perceived foreigners in Ecuador.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant suggested 2014 threats and bottle-breaking incident may relate to Discotheque business.
propositions.quote: He offered the possibility that the events in 2014, when a man broke a bottle outside his clothing store and threatened to kill him because he was an Arab and when two men later came into his clothing store with threats to harm him, may have been related to the Disco business.

propositions.text: No further events until 1.5 years later; Appellants could not connect text message to incidents or reasons for targeting.
propositions.quote: There were no further events until more than 1.5 years later, when the text message was sent to the Principal Appellant. The Appellants did not connect that text message to other incidents or to any specific reason for targeting: the Principal Appellant was asked but could offer no insight as to why he received that text or the reason for any of the other incidents of harm or threats of harm against himself and his family.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found 'Arab' is broadly used against foreigners; Appellants confirmed random violence and could not link incidents to specific targeting.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with Appellants' argument that scarce country documents mean higher discrimination risk for them.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's argue that the member erred in relying on scarce country condition documentation to support her conclusions but I disagree.

propositions.text: Lack of country info on personal attributes does not imply higher discrimination than groups identified as vulnerable.
propositions.quote: It does not logically follow that a lack of information about the specific personal attributes of the Appellants should mean that they experience higher levels of discrimination than the groups who are specifically identified in country condition documents as vulnerable groups in Ecuador.

propositions.text: Random or general violence with racial undertones can be distinguished from targeted persecution for a nexus ground.
propositions.quote: Furthermore and in any event, random or general violence that has a racial undertone is not an inconsistent concept and can be reasonably distinguished from targeted persecution toward the Appellants for a nexus ground.

propositions.text: Racist slurs suggest perpetrator's thoughts but do not suffice to infer persecutory harm for a nexus ground.
propositions.quote: An act of violence accompanied by racist slurs offers some suggestion about the perpetrator's thoughts or motivation but that part of the conduct is not sufficient to make an inference of persecutory harm toward the Appellants for a nexus ground.

propositions.text: Incidents align more with random violence or discrimination than targeted harm, except possibly related to business practice denying gang entry.
propositions.quote: Other than connection with the Principal Appellant's business practice of denying entry of gang or gang-appearing persons into his Discotheque, the incidents described by the Appellants are more consistent with random violence or discrimination than with specifically targeted harm toward them.

propositions.text: No country documents reference specific category of Muslims from Afghanistan perceived as Arabs; Appellants did not point to such reference.
propositions.quote: I have searched for information and not found specific reference in the country documents to the specific category of Muslims from Afghanistan who are perceived as Arabs, nor have the Appellants pointed out such reference.

propositions.text: Absence of specific profile in country documents does not imply persecution rather than generalized violence or discrimination.
propositions.quote: Thus, it may be true that the profile of the Appellants is not specifically canvassed in the country condition information. However, that fact does not demand an inference that their victimization is persecution rather than the generalized random violence or discrimination facing other residents of Ecuador.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds lack of country info does not imply higher discrimination; incidents align with random violence, not targeted persecution.

propositions.text: Persecution differs from discrimination by degree of seriousness; repeated or systematic cruelty or fundamental human dignity violation may be persecution.
propositions.quote: The difference between persecution, which may form the basis for refugee protection, and discrimination or harassment, which does not, is the degree of seriousness of the harm. To make the distinction, I considered the perpetrator's actions and their effect because, typically, it cannot be known what was in the minds of the perpetrators. Events may amount to persecution if cruelty was inflicted repeatedly and persistently or in a systematic way, for a nexus ground. Repetition is not necessary, however, as in some cases the serious quality of specific incidents will constitute a fundamental violation of human dignity.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains persecution differs from discrimination by seriousness, repetition, or fundamental human dignity violation.

propositions.text: Appellants suffered discrimination and random violence common in Ecuador; RPD weighed evidence correctly distinguishing from generalized risks.
propositions.quote: My own examination of events the Appellants have credibly described is that they have suffered a type of discrimination and random violence generally present in Ecuador. I find that the evidence was weighed correctly by the RPD member, who considered seriousness and looked for systematic indicators in an effort to distinguish what the Appellants experienced from the generalized risks affecting all residents of Ecuador.

propositions.text: RPD extensively questioned Appellants about possible targeting; no specifics found; Appellants attributed events to random violence or business practice.
propositions.quote: During the RPD hearing, the member enquired extensively of each of the adult Appellants if they had a sense or idea who might have targeted them and no specifics were forthcoming: each Appellant suggested general or random violence, accidental harm or, to a limited extent, that some events may have been a response to the business practice of denying entry to those perceived as gang members.

propositions.text: Evidence about events is more consistent with random violence than specific targeting except related to business practice discrimination.
propositions.quote: In totality, the evidence about specific events and incidents is more consistent with random violence than with specific targeting other than in relation to the business practice of the Principal Appellant, which was also generalized and non-specific discrimination.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Appellants suffered discrimination and random violence; RPD correctly distinguished from generalized risks and found no specific targeting.

propositions.text: Appellants argue police are ineffective and cannot protect them.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argued that they cannot rely on the police and do not have confidence the police can protect them

propositions.text: Court finds Appellants' perception of police ineffectiveness is subjective and unsupported by evidence.
propositions.quote: but that is not supported by the evidence. ... The perception of the Appellants that they do not have police support is subjective and not supported by the evidence.

propositions.text: Police inability to apprehend perpetrators does not equate to persecution or raise incident seriousness to persecution level.
propositions.quote: They have inferred police ineffectiveness from the fact that police did not identify and apprehend perpetrators but that is not sound logic. The inability of police to apprehend or identify perpetrators does not equate to persecution or harm or raise the seriousness of the reported incidents to a level of persecution.

propositions.text: Second Associated Appellant reported vandalism twice; police responded, took info, and searched for thieves; treated him respectfully.
propositions.quote: The Second Associated Appellant's evidence was that on the two occasions when he reported vandalism incidents to police, they responded, took information, and looked for the thieves. He confirmed that the police responded to his calls as they would respond for anyone in Ecuador and that they treated him respectfully.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant had positive police experience after reporting vandalism and threats at business.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant had a similarly positive experience when the police attended at his place of business after his report of vandalism and threats.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects Appellants' claim police are ineffective, finding police responded respectfully and appropriately to reports.

propositions.text: Appellants did not establish beating was personal targeting or future persecution risk; police treated Second Associated Appellant respectfully and equally.
propositions.quote: The Appellants did not establish that the beating incident against the Second Associated Appellant was personal targeting or that he would be persecuted in the future. They confirmed that he did not have trouble with teachers or public services, admission to university, treatment from professors, or access to public services because of a perceived nationality as Arab or for his ethnicity or religion. He confirmed that on two previous occasions when he called the police they responded, took information and searched for the perpetrators. They treated him with respect. They did not treat him differently from how other people in Ecuador are treated by police.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant's experience confirmed police effectiveness; family enjoyed economic stability, access to services, and religious freedom.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant's experience also confirmed the effectiveness of local police. The Appellants testified that the police responded to reported incidents of harm and vandalism respectfully and with follow-up investigations and they have enjoyed economic stability and success, access to all services, schools, and other personal and economic freedoms including the ability to attend mosque.

propositions.text: Evidence does not disclose systematic or institutional discrimination or personal risk of harm or torture for Convention ground.
propositions.quote: The evidence about his experience does not disclose systematic or institutional discrimination for a Convention ground or that he is personally at risk of harm or torture in Ecuador.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no personal targeting or persecution risk; police treated Appellants respectfully; no systematic discrimination or risk found.

propositions.text: Burden is on Appellants to show violence or discrimination amounts to persecution; lack of specific profile in country documents does not discharge burden.
propositions.quote: The burden was on the Appellants to show that the violence or discrimination toward them amounts to persecution. That burden is not discharged by simply pointing out that their unique profile is not specifically identified in the country documents.

propositions.text: Appellants acknowledged random generalized violence in Ecuador but did not identify specific, systematic, or sustained acts of discrimination or harm due to unique profile.
propositions.quote: They acknowledged that a random and generalized type of violence exists in Ecuador but have not identified specific, systematic or sustained acts of discrimination or harm because of their unique profile such that they are set apart from and not simply subject to the general risk of violence that affects everyone living in Ecuador.

paragraphs.summary: The court states burden is on Appellants to prove persecution; they failed to identify specific systematic discrimination beyond general violence.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred attributing 2013-2017 threats and attacks to Discotheque business denial of gang entry, as incidents occurred after closure.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that it was an error for the Member to attribute the 2013 to 2017 threats and violent incidents to his denying entry to gang members at the Discotheque because of events that happened after the Discotheque was closed: there was a shooting in 2014 when his wife was hurt and a death threat in 2016.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue RPD erred attributing post-closure threats and attacks to Discotheque business denial of gang entry.

propositions.text: Review of hearing audio shows Principal Appellant suggested 2014 and 2017 incidents might relate to Discotheque and Colombian gangs.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant testified that he did not know who shot at him and hit his wife in the 2014 incident, or who was responsible for the 2017 incidents, but himself suggested that it might have related to the Discotheque business and Colombian gangs.

propositions.text: Even if post-2013 events were random and unrelated to Discotheque, less evidence supports persecution than random generalized risk in Ecuador.
propositions.quote: Furthermore and in any event, even if the events after 2013 were randomly motivated incidents not connected to the operation of the Discotheque, there is less rather than more probative evidence that the events are persecutory rather than random generalized risk affecting all residents of Ecuador.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Principal Appellant suggested incidents might relate to Discotheque; even if unrelated, less evidence supports persecution than random risk.

propositions.text: Appellants' argument does not disclose error in RPD decision; member acknowledged racism but found discrimination, not persecution.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's argument does not disclose any error in the RPD member's decision. The member acknowledged that racism played a part in the events but found that this was discrimination, not persecution, which leads to the next argument.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes Appellants' argument shows no error; RPD acknowledged racism but found discrimination, not persecution.

propositions.text: Appellants allege RPD improperly dismissed physical violence and attacks as not racially motivated, thus denying persecution.
propositions.quote: The Appellants allege that the RPD member improperly dismissed the physical violence and attacks against the parents and against their adult son as not being racially motivated. They argue that by doing so, the member was able to find that the racist comments and anti-Muslim words against the Appellants did not rise to the level of persecution.

propositions.text: Appellants argue combined physical attacks and racist comments show persecution and future risk on Convention grounds.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that, when the physical attacks and death threats are taken together with the daily racist and anti-Muslim comments, there is no doubt that the Appellants experienced persecution and are at risk of being persecuted in the future on Convention grounds.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants allege RPD dismissed racially motivated violence and comments, denying persecution despite combined evidence.

propositions.text: Court disagrees; RPD did not err in persecution vs. discrimination analysis; persecution is sustained or systemic fundamental rights violation.
propositions.quote: I disagree with the Appellants' position and find that the RPD member did not err in her analysis of persecution vs. discrimination. Persecution is sustained or systemic violation of basic human rights in a fundamental way.

propositions.text: RPD noted Appellants not denied education, healthcare, housing; Principal Appellant operates businesses; family enjoys freedoms including religious practice and social participation.
propositions.quote: The member took note that the Appellants have not been denied access to education, healthcare, or the ability to rent or purchase accommodation in Ecuador, since arriving there in 2000. The Principal Appellant has not been prevented from operating his businesses and the family has enjoyed financial and economic success. They are not prevented from practising their religion. The children participate socially and are not ostracized as Muslims, Arabs or Afghan children.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with Appellants, finding RPD correctly distinguished persecution from discrimination based on fundamental rights and freedoms enjoyed.

propositions.text: The Appellants have suffered discrimination but not persecution.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have suffered discrimination but not persecution.

propositions.text: Evidence does not show reasonable chance or serious possibility of persecution going forward.
propositions.quote: Looking forward, the evidence does not show reasonable chance or serious possibility of persecution.

propositions.text: The RPD member noted a general risk of violence in Ecuador and that the Appellants' risk is not different from others in Ecuador.
propositions.quote: The RPD member took note, and I agree, that there is a general risk of violence in Ecuador and that the risk faced by the Appellants is not different from what others face in Ecuador.

propositions.text: The Appellants have not shown the RPD member's analysis was incorrect or that evidence leads to persecution rather than discrimination.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have not shown how the RPD member's analysis was incorrect or that the evidence leads to conclusion of persecution rather than discrimination.

propositions.text: The member's finding that the Appellants did not take steps to protect themselves is unfounded.
propositions.quote: Argument e) the member's finding that the Appellants did not take steps to protection themselves is unfounded

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellants suffered discrimination, not persecution, agrees with the RPD's risk assessment, and notes the Appellants' argument that the member erred on protection steps.

propositions.text: The member was wrong to say the Appellants did not take steps to protect themselves due to fear as Muslims or perceived Arabs or refugees.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the member was wrong to say that the Appellants "don't take steps to protect themselves because they're afraid, as Muslims, or perceived to [be] Arabs or refugees".

propositions.text: The Appellant closed his business, contacted police many times, armed himself with a pistol, and the family left Ecuador.
propositions.quote: They point out that the Appellant closed his business, that they contacted the police on many occasions to protect themselves, that the Appellant armed himself with a pistol, and that the family eventually left Ecuador.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue the member erred about their protective actions, citing business closure, police contact, arming, and leaving Ecuador.

propositions.text: The Appellants took the RPD member's statement out of context regarding protection steps and religious practice interference.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have taken the RPD member's statement out of context.

propositions.text: The member found no systemic discrimination interfering with the Appellants' fundamental human right to practice religion.
propositions.quote: The member was evaluating whether their fundamental human right to practise their religion was interfered with and found that they did not face systemic discrimination in that regard.

propositions.text: The member noted the Appellants were not prevented from practicing religion or advertising business, children were not ostracized, and family did not protect themselves out of fear of those attributes.
propositions.quote: The Member pointed out that the Appellants were not prevented them from openly practising their religion or advertising their business, that the children were not ostracized because of being Muslim or Afghan or perceived as Arab, and pointed out that the family did not take steps to protect themselves out of fear because of those attributes.

propositions.text: The Appellants experienced discrimination or random attacks common in Ecuador, not persecution.
propositions.quote: This is not to say that the Appellants did not experience incidents of discrimination or random attacks such as occur generally in Ecuador.

propositions.text: Distinction between persecution and discrimination requires evaluating evidence with country conditions, which the RPD member did correctly.
propositions.quote: As previously discussed, the distinction between persecution and discrimination includes a need to evaluate and characterize evidence about past events and experiences taking into consideration the country conditions, which the RPD member did correctly in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellants misinterpret the RPD member's context, who found no systemic religious discrimination and correctly distinguished persecution from discrimination.

propositions.text: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under IRPA section 111(1)(a).
propositions.quote: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision that the Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection under IRPA.
